title: State Pattern
oneLiner: Lets an object change its behavior automatically when its internal state changes, by delegating to a state-specific object instead of one giant switch statement.

hero.name: Morph
hero.catchphrase: I don't check what state I'm in — I simply become it.
hero.power: Delegates behavior entirely to the current state object, so switching states automatically switches behavior.
hero.weakness: Every discrete state becomes its own small class — for a simple two-state toggle, that's more ceremony than a boolean flag needs.
hero.origin: Morph appeared inside a vending machine's `dispense()` method, which had grown a 15-branch switch statement checking `state === "idle" | "hasCoin" | "dispensing" | "sold out"` at every single method.

story.problem: VendingMachine's `insertCoin()`, `selectItem()`, and `dispense()` methods each start with a switch on `this.state`. Every new state means editing every single method to add a new branch.
story.solution: Morph gives each state (Idle, HasCoin, Dispensing, SoldOut) its own class implementing the same `VendingMachineState` interface. The machine just delegates to `this.state.insertCoin()`.
story.result: Adding a new state means adding one new class implementing the interface. No existing method needs to grow another switch branch.

before: Every method starts with a switch on the current state
Adding a state means editing every existing method
Invalid transitions are easy to allow by accident
after: Each state is a self-contained class implementing one interface
Adding a state means adding one new class
Invalid transitions are simply not implemented in that state's class

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: Three methods each start with the same 15-branch switch statement on the machine's state.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We're adding a 'maintenance mode' state. That means editing this switch statement in FIVE different methods, again.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: Morph appears, shifting fluidly between four distinct forms — Idle, HasCoin, Dispensing, SoldOut.
panels.speaker: Morph
panels.dialogue: Stop checking what state you're in everywhere. Let the state itself decide how to behave — delegate, don't branch.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: Each state implements insertCoin(), selectItem(), dispense(). The machine just calls this.state.insertCoin().
panels.speaker: Morph
panels.dialogue: The machine doesn't check what state it's in anymore. It just asks the current state to handle the call — and the state knows exactly what to do, or refuse to do.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: MaintenanceState ships as one new file. Every existing state class is untouched.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: One new class, zero edits to the four existing states. The switch statements are just gone.

useWhen: An object's behavior changes significantly based on an internal state, and that logic is scattered across many switch/if statements.
You have well-defined states with clear transition rules between them.
You want invalid state transitions to be structurally impossible rather than checked at runtime everywhere.
avoidWhen: There are only two states (a simple boolean flag) — a full State pattern is unnecessary ceremony.
State transitions are rare or trivial, and a switch statement is genuinely easier to read in one place.
The states don't actually have distinct behavior, just distinct data — that's not really a State problem.
commonMistakes: Applying State to a simple two-value toggle where a boolean and an if-statement would be clearer.
Letting state classes directly reference and mutate each other in tangled ways instead of going through the context object.
Forgetting to make invalid transitions explicit (e.g. `dispense()` called while `Idle`) — silently ignoring them hides bugs.
Confusing State with Strategy — State transitions are driven by the object itself; Strategy is chosen by the client.
explanation.realWorldExample: TCP connection state machines (Listen, SynSent, Established, Closed), traffic light controllers, order-processing pipelines (Pending, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled), and UI component state (Loading, Loaded, Error) are all classic State pattern use cases.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: This looks identical to Strategy — swap in an object, behavior changes.

conversation.speaker: Morph
conversation.message: Structurally close cousins, but who's driving matters. With Strategy, the CLIENT picks an algorithm. With me, the OBJECT ITSELF transitions between states as things happen — insertCoin() moves me from Idle to HasCoin automatically.

conversation.speaker: Morph
conversation.message: When there are really just two states — on and off. A boolean handles that fine. I earn my keep once there are three or more states with real behavioral differences and transition rules.

codeBattle.scenario: Your order-processing system has Pending, Paid, Shipped, Delivered, and Cancelled states, each allowing only specific transitions, and the transition-checking logic is duplicated across six different methods.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: Morph gives each order status its own class that knows exactly which transitions are valid from it, eliminating the duplicated switch logic across every method.

quiz.question: What triggers a state transition in the State pattern?
options: The object itself, in response to something that happens to it
The client code, choosing which state to use ahead of time
quiz.answer: The object itself, in response to something that happens to it
quiz.explanation: The defining trait of State is that the object drives its own transitions as events occur.

quiz.question: How does State typically eliminate switch-statement sprawl?
options: Each state becomes its own class implementing a shared interface, and the object delegates to whichever state it currently holds
By deleting all conditional logic from the codebase entirely
By storing all states in a single database table
quiz.answer: Each state becomes its own class implementing a shared interface, and the object delegates to whichever state it currently holds
quiz.explanation: Delegation to a state object replaces repeated 'if state is X' checks scattered across methods.

quiz.question: When is State overkill?
options: When there are only two states, well-modeled by a simple boolean flag
When there are five or more states with distinct behavior
When transition rules between states are complex
When state-specific behavior is scattered across many methods
quiz.answer: When there are only two states, well-modeled by a simple boolean flag
quiz.explanation: A boolean and an if-statement is simpler and clearer for a genuine two-value toggle.

quiz.question: How does State differ from Strategy?
options: In State, the object transitions itself between states; in Strategy, the client chooses which algorithm to use
State can only have one implementation; Strategy can have many
They are identical patterns with different names
Strategy requires inheritance, State forbids it
quiz.answer: In State, the object transitions itself between states; in Strategy, the client chooses which algorithm to use
quiz.explanation: The structural shape is similar, but who drives the swap — and why — is what separates the two patterns.
